Chapter One: A Country on the Edge – Everyday Life Before the Storm
It’s easy to see a place as just another headline on the news... but before the world turned its gaze to Rwanda, life there was filled with simple, everyday routines.
Picture this: people waking up to the crow of a rooster, kids rushing off to school, and neighbors greeting each other along dusty roads. The hills stretched out, lush and green, and the air carried the smoky scent of breakfast fires. For most folks, life felt like a patchwork of small hopes and daily struggles—nothing out of the ordinary, nothing that hinted at the darkness waiting ahead.
But if you looked a little closer, there was a tension simmering beneath the surface—something most outsiders would never notice.
In the busy markets, people traded not just goods but glances—sometimes friendly, sometimes a bit guarded, depending on who stood across the stall.
Rwanda’s history, shaped by cycles of violence and uneasy peace, lingered quietly in every conversation. Some remembered stories their parents told about violence from years before, but for many, those memories felt more like distant shadows than real threats.
In one small village, a teacher tried to keep her students focused, even as rumors drifted in from the capital. She could see some kids were distracted, their eyes flicking to the door whenever a sound broke the silence. At home, her husband listened to the radio, brow furrowed, picking up on subtle changes—broadcasts that suddenly seemed heavier, warnings that felt less like news and more like threats.
Still, most people clung to their routines, hoping normal life could keep the troubles at bay.
A farmer checked his fields each morning, measuring the season’s progress by how tall his crops had grown.
A shopkeeper swept his storefront, chatting with customers about the price of beans. Even as political speeches grew sharper and the government tightened its grip, life carried on—as if simply living could hold back the tide.
But the warning signs were there if you paid attention.
The government’s language became more divisive, and radio stations—which used to play music and friendly chatter—started repeating messages that set neighbor against neighbor.
Some families quietly made backup plans, sending their kids to stay with relatives in the countryside, just in case. Others brushed off the warnings, certain that nothing could shatter the fragile peace they’d known for years.
It’s strange, isn’t it, how quickly the ordinary can slip into the extraordinary?
One day, a family’s gathered around the table, laughing over dinner. The next, they’re huddled in fear, listening for footsteps outside their door.
The switch from normal life to chaos wasn’t sudden—it crept in slowly, a growing sense of dread that finally broke through.
Looking back now, it’s clear the seeds of violence had been planted long before the world started to pay attention.
The divisions between Hutu and Tutsi—widened by years of colonial rule and political manipulation—had never really healed. The government’s campaign to dehumanize the Tutsi minority, using both propaganda and policy, set the stage for what was coming.
Most people didn’t see themselves as part of some grand historical moment—they were just trying to get by.
But history, as it often does, had other plans.
